title: Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Restores American Saltwater Angling and Recreation
text: Fact Sheets Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Restores American Saltwater Angling and Recreation The White House September 17, 2026 MODERNIZING MANAGEMENT AND EXPANDING PUBLIC ACCESS: Today, President Donald J. Trump signed an Executive Order to modernize Federal fisheries management, empower recreational industries, and eliminate unnecessary restrictions on American boaters and anglers. The Order reduces administrative burdens by directing the Secretary of Commerce, the Secretary of Agriculture, and the Secretary of the Interior to initiate actions to suspend, revise, or rescind regulations that overly burden boaters, anglers, and outdoor businesses. Relevant agencies will also seek to transition to multi-year permitting for compliant charter operators and outdoor businesses, with a standard presumption of renewal. The Order modernizes fisheries science by directing the Secretary of Commerce to transition from mail-in surveys to mobile electronic catch reporting apps, improving data accuracy and preventing improper access restrictions on anglers; mandating a 5-year strategic plan to integrate recreational economic data into seasonal quota decisions; and calling for the development of a real-time depredation reporting protocol via mobile app. The Order directs the Secretary of Commerce to launch pilot programs for depleted stocks, including Atlantic Striped Bass, and streamline applicable Trust Fund projects to directly boost fish populations. The Order promotes healthy habitats by directing the Secretary of the Interior to create the Federal Outer Continental Shelf Reef-in-Place Program to use decommissioned oil and gas platforms to support artificial reefs; directing the Make America Beautiful Again (MABA) Commission to establish a Restoration Coordination Working Group to streamline habitat restoration efforts and ensure efficient use of Federal resources across agencies; and directing the Secretary of State, the Secretary of Commerce, and the Secretary of the Interior, along with the United States Trade Representative to remove barriers to sustainable shark fisheries. ELEVATING RECREATIONAL FISHING IN NATIONAL POLICY: President Trump is committed to removing unnecessary restrictions on saltwater anglers, offshore boaters, and charter operators in order to enhance domestic outdoor recreation, support American jobs, and strengthen coastal economies. America’s outdoor recreation sector generates over $1.2 trillion annually and supports over 5 million jobs, with recreational fishing being a primary driver. Federal fisheries management has historically prioritized restricting access over empowering affiliated industries, burdening charter businesses and limiting public access to marine resources. Prohibiting or restricting recreational access is unnecessary for proper management when State-level partnerships and modernized data collection can provide accurate, real-time information for responsible oversight. This action sets a clear policy to elevate the importance of marine recreational fishing across Federal ocean, coastal, and public land decision-making. DELIVERING HISTORIC ACTION FOR AMERICAN FISHERIES: President Trump is fulfilling his commitment to revitalizing the Nation’s maritime economy, reversing federal overreach, and prioritizing American fishing interests. On his first day back in office, President Trump signed a Presidential Memorandum pausing offshore wind energy projects to preserve a robust U.S. fishing industry. In April 2025, February 2026, and June 2026, President Trump issued proclamations restoring fishing access in all Marine National Monuments. In April 2025, President Trump signed an Executive Order restoring seafood competitiveness through deregulation, enhancing domestic seafood production, and establishing the America First Seafood Strategy. In July 2025, President Trump signed an Executive Order establishing the MABA Commission, to conserve America’s lands and waters, cut red tape, and drive conservation and economic growth. Through the strategic use of the Magnuson-Stevens Act and executive action, NOAA has successfully deregulated fishing operations, reversed decades-old closures, and maximized harvest quotas. NOAA expedited the openings of fisheries and increased catch limits based on the best available science, delivering financial returns to coastal communities. NOAA continues to aggressively slash red tape and replace outdated, micromanaged restrictions with adaptive, flexible standards – maximizing profitability for the domestic fleet and keeping fisheries open. Through his leadership, President Trump continues to fulfill his promises to undo burdensome regulations, empower State-Federal partnerships, and restore access to America’s coastal waters. These actions have unlocked billions of dollars in economic value and strengthened the outdoor recreation economy.

title: Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Reinvigorates America’s Hunting Heritage
text: Fact Sheets Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Reinvigorates America’s Hunting Heritage The White House September 17, 2026 EXPANDING ACCESS AND PROMOTING AMERICA’S HUNTING HERITAGE: Today, President Donald J. Trump signed an Executive Order to expand access to America’s public lands and waterways, foster and recruit the next generation of hunters, and promote robust and healthy wild game populations. The Order directs the Secretary of the Interior to expand hunting opportunities in select federal lands that would not put objects of historic and scientific interest at risk. The Order directs the Secretary of the Interior, the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of War, and the Secretary of Commerce to propose changes to polices that prevent access of public lands for recreation, infrastructure repair, and wildlife management, as well as to encourage volunteers to manage wildlife populations and invasive species, allow the use assistive technology on access trails and hunting locations for people with disabilities, and allow the use of traditional lead ammo and tackle. The Order directs the Secretary of the Interior, the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of War, and the Secretary of Commerce to unlock checkerboarded and landlocked parcels through voluntary access easements, land exchanges, and cooperative agreements that respect private property rights. The Order directs the Secretary of Agriculture to review and reform high-demand Forest Service-administered river access lotteries to prioritize United States citizens and prior applicants who haven’t previously received access via lottery, and to prohibit automatic computer entries. The Order directs the Secretary of the Interior to streamline regulations for authorizing seasonal migratory game bird hunting and to encourage States to promote and expand Sunday hunting on State and Federal lands. The Order directs the Secretary of Labor, the Secretary of Education, the Secretary of the Interior, and the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to identify, clarify, and prioritize opportunities and incentives to cultivate the hunting tradition in young Americans and veterans using existing Federal funding and authorities. The Order directs the Secretary of War, the Secretary of the Interior, and the Secretary of Agriculture to coordinate with States to align management practices and conservation plans in order to promote the growth of critical game species populations. The Order directs the Secretary of Agriculture and the Secretary of the Interior to support and encourage States to increase wild game donations for consumption in schools, food banks, and the Emergency Food Assistance Program. CUTTING RED TAPE TO RESTORE AMERICA’S HUNTING TRADITION: President Trump is cutting red tape, rolling back restrictions, and expanding hunting opportunities for Americans. Hunting drives healthy and abundant animal populations, conserves our beautiful wildlife for future generations, and ensures that every American can enjoy our rugged, diverse, and untamed frontiers. Due to years of overregulation by other administrations, until President Trump’s actions, accessing hunting had never been more difficult. Hunting opportunities in the United States have declined due to Federal regulatory overreach, confusing and inconsistent policies, and heavy-handed restrictions. America’s hunting heritage must be reinvigorated, protected, and expanded to benefit Americans. American hunters and anglers need better access to our nation’s lands and the next generation of Americans must have the opportunity to share in our nation’s rich sporting heritage. REIGNING IN GOVERNMENT OVERREACH: President Trump is restoring access to Federal lands while conserving and protecting America’s natural resources. During President Trump’s first term, he signed the Great American Outdoors Act—the single largest investment in America’s national parks and public lands in history and the most significant conservation achievement since Teddy Roosevelt’s presidency. By the end of President Trump’s first term, his Administration designated 1.3 million new acres of wilderness, added 1,645 miles of new trails to the National Recreational Trails System, and expanded hunting and fishing opportunities across more than 2.3 million acres of land. Immediately upon returning to office, President Trump signed an Executive Order to Unleash American Energy that opened hundreds of millions of acres of Federal lands and waters to energy development and streamlined permitting to increase production of reliable and affordable energy. In February 2025, President Trump’s Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) rescinded its NEPA regulations, clearing the way for CEQ to lead individual agencies as they reformed their own NEPA policies in order to eliminate unnecessary red tape and speed environmental review for permits and other government actions. In July 2025, President Trump signed an Executive Order establishing the Make America Beautiful Again (MABA) Commission to conserve America’s lands and waters, cut red tape, and drive conservation and economic growth. In July 2026, the MABA Commission issued its midterm report to ensure that our Nation’s next 250 years are beautiful, successful, and secure. In May 2026, Department of the Interior rescinded the Bureau of Land Management’s Public Lands Rule, reaffirming the commitment to restoring balance in Federal land management by prioritizing multiple use access, elevating local decision-making, and supporting responsible energy development, ranching, grazing, timber production, and recreation. In May 2026, President Trump signed an Executive Order rescinding outdated restrictions on access to Federal lands, restoring balanced land management and reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens. In August 2026, the Department of Agriculture took action to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule that prevents road construction, reconstruction, and timber harvest on nearly 45 million acres of the National Forest System.

title: Joint Task Force Southern Border Soldiers Innovate to Reinforce Barriers
text: Border Barrier Soldiers assigned to Joint Task Force Southern Border, supporting Operation Ardent Vanguard, place concertina wire on top of Hesco barriers at National Defense Area 2 near Fort Hancock, Texas, Aug. 6, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 3.99 MB ) Credit: Army Spc. Sean Hoch VIRIN: 260806-A-MA561-9014 Soldiers with the 62nd Engineer Battalion, 36th Engineer Brigade, assigned to Joint Task Force Southern Border in support of Operation Ardent Vanguard, recently reinforced a challenging section of the southern border barrier. The soldiers emplaced two strands of concertina wire and one strand of razor wire atop 7-foot Hesco barriers in National Defense Area 2 near Fort Hancock, Texas. The reinforced barriers disrupt climbing attempts and enhance persistent detection, monitoring and rapid response along high-risk border corridors. "Barrier reinforcement operations represent more than physical infrastructure; they showcase the technical ingenuity and skill of our service members," said Army Maj. Gen. Curtis Taylor, commander of Joint Task Force Southern Border and the 1st Armored Division and Fort Bliss, Texas. "For the last 14 weeks, our great soldiers have been out here day and night developing innovative solutions to stop human trafficking in our own territory." In May, the Navy and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers began installing 10 miles of barriers under orders from the War Department and U.S. Northern Command. Within about 30 days, they constructed 10 miles of barriers, including site preparation, mobilization, environmental clearance, receiving barrier sections from overseas, and transporting more than 90,000 cubic yards of fill material. On average, constructing 10 miles of Hesco barriers takes approximately 28 days when crews work 12-hour shifts. However, this timeline does not include mobilization, land clearing or compaction. During the recent reinforcement operation, soldiers assigned to the 591st Combat Engineer Company-Infantry, 62nd Engineer Battalion, maintained a demanding pace as they reinforced barriers from Santa Teresa, New Mexico, to Fort Hancock, Texas. "When we work on border reinforcement operations, we typically start in the morning, and then we work until around midafternoon," said Army 2nd Lt. Jonah Posada, a Sapper platoon leader with the 591st. "And then, we'll return to Fort Bliss and prepare for the next day; we try to continue at that pace for the whole week." To address site conditions and avoid the Texas summer heat, the company adopted an offset work schedule: one platoon began work in the early evening; another relieved it and worked until late morning. The elevated work surface and limited workspace made installing razor wire on the Hesco barriers difficult. Additionally, the soldiers could not use metal stakes, which are generally used for support, because they would place compressive stress on the barriers. Instead, they used boom lifts as work platforms to emplace razor wire atop the concertina wire. The final 300-meter section presented another significant challenge: soft, uneven terrain prevented the boom lifts from reaching the area and attempts to move the equipment left them stuck. Rather than leave the section unfinished, the 591st soldiers developed a solution using equipment already available. {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} "We devised a plan using tent poles and rope that we had in our high-angle mountaineering kit," Posada said. "Using those ropes, we stretched [the section of wire] out and kept tension on the razor wire." Soldiers on the ground used camouflage-net poles to lift the razor wire while teams atop the barrier secured it in place. A carabiner attached to a rope helped lift the wire from the ground, enabling the soldiers to complete the final section without relying on boom lifts. The solution was the latest in a series of adaptations soldiers developed as they transitioned between traditional barrier work and reinforcing Hesco barriers. The Hesco barriers introduced additional challenges because the razor wire configuration was not standard for the engineers. "The actual obstacle that we emplaced on top of the Hesco [barriers] is not normal," Posada said. "We had to figure out how to best overcome that. The terrain by the Hesco was a big hindrance on the mission as well." The company also developed techniques to prevent injuries. In one method, the soldiers attached a wooden post to a boom lift and used it to position the wire across the barrier. The completed work reinforces the barrier with additional obstacles intended to deter unauthorized crossings and support the broader border-security mission. Posada said the U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents appreciated the efforts and noted that the additional barriers helped limit crossings. The operation underscores the role of combat engineers in providing practical solutions when terrain, equipment and mission requirements intersect. For the soldiers conducting the work, the operation demonstrated the importance of adapting established engineering practices to conditions on the ground. Posada said he shared the techniques that his platoon developed with other platoon leaders in the company so they could apply the lessons learned to similar missions. Spotlight: DOW Support to the Southern Border

title: NORAD F-16s Deploy to High North Under Operation Arctic Vanguard
text: Arctic Formation U.S. Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcon aircraft and a KC-135 Stratotanker fly in formation while conducting aerial refueling as part of Operation Arctic Vanguard over Greenland, Sept. 16, 2026. The operation is a joint and multinational effort designed to enhance interoperability, test cold-weather combat readiness and strengthen coalition capabilities across the Arctic. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 2.05 MB ) Credit: Air Force Maj. David Brown VIRIN: 260916-D-D0962-9549 The Alaskan North American Aerospace Defense Command Region deployed F-16 Fighting Falcons from Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, to Goose Bay, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, in support of Operation Arctic Vanguard 26-4.2. During this NORAD operation, Alaskan NORAD Region is operating directly alongside the Canadian NORAD Region to execute critical defense missions across the Arctic, Sept. 13-26. Under Arctic Vanguard, NORAD personnel and aircraft will forward deploy into Greenland to execute operations in austere conditions alongside partners from Denmark and other NATO countries. This operation supports the NORAD and U.S. Northern Command Nordic Bridge concept, which aligns the commands' Arctic operations, exercises and training, activities and investments with other U.S. combatant commands, NATO, individual nations and regional partners. "Operation Arctic Vanguard demonstrates that austere conditions and vast distances present no barrier to NORAD's collective defense," said Air Force Lt. Gen. Robert D. Davis, commander, Alaskan NORAD Region. "Deploying combat airpower from Alaska across Canada and forward into Greenland validates our agile combat capabilities and demonstrates our seamless integration with the Canadian NORAD region, the Kingdom of Denmark and our NATO allies. Together, we maintain continuous vigilance and credible deterrence across North America's northern approaches." {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} Operation Arctic Vanguard is part of a recurring series of NORAD and Northcom operations conducted across the North American Arctic region to enhance presence, operate from forward Arctic locations and defend North America's northern approaches. Under the Nordic Bridge concept and efforts to bring orchestration to operations, activities and investments in the Arctic, Operation Arctic Vanguard enables more consistent presence of multinational forces in the region, operating in multiple domains and in varying locations. Spotlight: NATO

title: Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Restores Reciprocity in Government Procurement
text: Fact Sheets Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Restores Reciprocity in Government Procurement The White House September 16, 2026 ENDING CANADA’S UNFAIR ACCESS TO FEDERAL PROCUREMENT: Today, President Donald J. Trump signed a Presidential Memorandum to identify and take steps to remove Canadian-origin goods from Federal Civil Government Procurement in response to Canada’s measures that have denied U.S. firms access to Canada’s federal and provincial procurement markets. The Memorandum directs the Director of the Office of Management and Budget and the United States Trade Representative, in coordination with the Federal Acquisition Regulatory Council, to identify and take all steps toward removing or otherwise making non-available for purchase Canadian-origin items in the federal civil procurement system. The Memorandum also directs the United States Trade Representative to monitor Canada’s continued treatment of U.S. origin goods in Canadian government procurement. PUTTING AMERICA FIRST: President Trump is taking action to hold Canada accountable for its continued unreasonable and discriminatory treatment of U.S. goods, which has burdened and disadvantaged hardworking Americans. Canada has received preferential access to the U.S. market for years, while doubling down on and continuing its unfair treatment of U.S. commerce. Despite Canada’s procurement commitments to the United States, Canadian provinces have disadvantaged American small businesses and companies by, among other things, establishing preferences for Canadian products and content under the “Buy Canadian” policy. Meanwhile, Canadian companies have preferential access to over $280 billion of the U.S. government procurement system while U.S. companies no longer receive equal treatment in the Canadian government procurement system. PROTECTING AMERICAN WORKERS AND ENSURING FAIR TRADE: President Trump is continuing to deliver on his promise to keep American workers, farmers, and businesses first by ending other countries’ unfair and unreasonable trade practices against the United States. President Trump’s America First Trade Policy was created to benefit American workers and families and has dramatically expanded global market access for U.S. exports, strengthened workers’ incomes, reshored and supported American jobs, and reduced the trade deficit. The United States, under President Trump’s leadership, did not agree to renew the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) in its current form, because the deal is not sufficiently beneficial for U.S. manufacturers, farmers, ranchers, workers, service suppliers, and businesses of all sizes. Through negotiations with foreign trading partners and the strategic use of tariffs, President Trump has secured trillions in private and foreign investment to bring American jobs and manufacturing back to the United States while diversifying global supply chains and reducing dependence on adversarial nations. On September 8, 2026, President Trump banned and increased tariffs on certain products under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to address Canada’s continued discrimination against American exporters and to offset the disadvantage or burden on U.S. commerce from Canada’s discriminatory treatment against U.S. exports of alcoholic beverages, dairy, and motor vehicles.

title: DOW Hosts 2nd Interagency Summit to Strengthen Counter-Drone Defense
text: Joint Interagency Task Force 401 hosted its second interagency summit last month to accelerate cooperation against rapidly evolving drone threats. Drone Summit Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, Joint Interagency Task Force 401 director, speaks at an interagency summit in Alexandria, Va., Aug. 21, 2026. Hosted by JIATF 401, the summit accelerated whole-of-government cooperation against the rapidly evolving threat of unmanned aircraft systems. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 471.04 KB ) Credit: Army Lt. Col. Adam Scher VIRIN: 260821-A-MJ360-9316 The gathering brought together more than 200 leaders and experts from 75 departments and agencies to synchronize efforts to strengthen homeland defense against drones. The task force is the War Department's premier counter-unmanned aircraft agency. Building on the momentum following the first full year since it was established in August 2025, the summit emphasized growing interagency partnerships that are rapidly delivering counter-UAS capabilities to warfighters, federal partners and local law enforcement. "Drones have fundamentally changed the operational environment," said Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, JIATF 401 director. "To meet this challenge, we must outpace our adversaries by working together to deliver capabilities quickly. This summit is one way we are synchronizing a whole-of-government effort to secure our borders, defend the national airspace and protect the American people." Discussions primarily focused on establishing a unified, cross-domain common operating picture for air traffic in areas critical for national security. Participants also took part in collaborative breakout groups focused on five key areas of counter-UAS integration for homeland defense: Major-event and critical-infrastructure preparation; Reporting, jurisdiction and information sharing; Authorities, policy and legislation; Capability access and the counter-UAS marketplace; Testing, standards and integration. The summit allowed participants to identify challenges, share best practices and strengthen coordination across agencies, while also highlighting innovations in the counter-UAS marketplace pioneered by JIATF 401. Counter-Unmanned Aircraft Systems Summit From left, retired Air Force Gen. Glen D. Vanherck, former commander of U.S. Northern Command and North American Aerospace Defense Command; Jarred Conley, Defense Innovation Unit portfolio director; and Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, Joint Interagency Task Force 401 director, participate in a panel during a counter-unmanned aircraft systems summit at National Harbor, Md., Aug. 25, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 235.52 KB ) Credit: Army Lt. Col. Adam Scher VIRIN: 260825-A-MJ360-9247 It also highlighted the War Department's efforts to transition emerging counter-UAS technologies from testing toward operational employment. The task force is conducting a directed-energy pilot program at multiple military installations to evaluate high-energy lasers, high-power microwaves and other novel technologies in an operational environment. Together, these initiatives demonstrate JIATF 401's commitment to accelerating innovation, strengthening interagency partnerships and delivering effective counter-drone capabilities to the warfighter. "My charge for this summit is for each of you to walk away with specific actions to address problems," Ross said. "We are all in this together, and it will take all of us working together to effectively counter the threat of drones and keep our warfighters and the American people safe." The summit concluded with a unified commitment to maintain continuous interagency teamwork and information sharing. By aligning efforts across the department, interagency partners and federal agencies, JIATF 401 continues to cut through bureaucracy and rapidly deliver state-of-the-art counter-drone capabilities to warfighters worldwide. title: Southern Vanguard 2026 Turns Peruvian Jungle Into a Classroom
text: Wet Work U.S. soldiers assigned to the 551st Infantry Regiment perform jungle waterborne training during Exercise Southern Vanguard 26 in Sauce, Peru, Sept. 9, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 5.61 MB ) Credit: Army Sgt. Grace Wajler VIRIN: 260909-Z-DX231-9035 Movement slows. Equipment gets heavier. Water becomes an obstacle instead of a landmark. The environment quietly strips away assumptions about how quickly a formation should move or how easily a soldier can accomplish a familiar task. For U.S. soldiers training alongside Peruvian and Chilean forces during Exercise Southern Vanguard 26, that friction is exactly the point. In the hills surrounding Sauce, Peru, soldiers are learning to move, survive and operate in terrain where their Peruvian counterparts have spent years developing expertise. During the opening days of jungle warfare training, multinational formations started at various lanes, including amphibious movement, survival skills and small-unit tactics designed for an environment that can punish even routine movement. Jungle Portrait Army Capt. Jared Fonzi, an operations planner assigned to the 551st Infantry Regiment, U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Command, joins approximately 400 warfighters to execute Exercise Southern Vanguard 26 in Peru, Sept. 10, 2026. The field training and command post exercise takes place in a demanding, austere jungle environment and includes combined operations designed to simulate real-world contingencies in the complex terrain of the jungle hills of the Amazon. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 5.33 MB ) Credit: Army Staff Sgt. Mickey Miller VIRIN: 260910-Z-HY815-9036 "Multiply fatigue by 10," Army Capt. Jared Fonzi, an operations planner assigned to the 551st Infantry Regiment, U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Command, said while describing the physical effects of jungle operations. "The climate, the terrain, the physical exhaustion that everyone here goes through — pictures do not justify the stress and the physical fatigue." Southern Vanguard 26 is a multinational exercise hosted by the Peruvian Army and designed to strengthen interoperability among participating forces while building proficiency in jungle mobility, survivability and tactical operations. For American soldiers, participation offers something difficult to replicate at home: The opportunity to become students of a partner force operating in a terrain it understands intimately. Fonzi, a graduate of the Jungle Operations Training Course-Panama, Ranger School and an infantry officer proficient with conventional U.S. tactics, said jungle warfare changes the scale at which soldiers must think and maneuver. "The size of the maneuvering element is far smaller," he said. "You don't really maneuver as a platoon, which is usually the bread and butter of U.S. operations. Here, with smaller elements — team size, squad size — you need to rely more on individual survival techniques and minimal equipment." That emphasis places greater importance on survival, fieldcraft and understanding the environment itself. Humidity, elevation, water obstacles, rainfall and dense vegetation are not simply background conditions. "These climate differences and natural elements are what affect the fight," Fonzi said. That reality is also driving U.S. soldiers to look outward for expertise. {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} Fonzi said U.S. forces are relying heavily on jungle warfare specialists from countries such as Peru, Colombia and Panama to understand how forces accustomed to the environment operate and which techniques might improve U.S. tactics, techniques and procedures. The dynamic is visible throughout Southern Vanguard 26. Peruvian instructors are leading much of the jungle training, while U.S. instructors work alongside them and help translate techniques for American formations. Fonzi described the Peruvian approach as aggressive and immediate, often moving soldiers quickly from instruction into practical application. "There's really no crawl phase here," he said. "They'll give a brief instruction, and then they just throw them in the water or whatever training environment they go into." The approach may differ from how many American soldiers are accustomed to training, but adapting to unfamiliar methods is part of the exercise itself. Interoperability is often discussed in terms of radios, procedures and whether two formations can communicate on a battlefield. But before any of that works, soldiers have to understand how their partners think, move and solve problems. Sometimes that begins with something as unremarkable as getting everyone across a body of water. That process requires a certain humility. The U.S. military brings considerable capability nearly anywhere it goes. The jungle offers a useful reminder that capability and expertise are not the same thing. Sometimes readiness means arriving prepared to teach. Other times, it means recognizing when someone else has something to teach you. Southern Vanguard creates room for both. For soldiers operating beneath the jungle canopy, the lessons are as physical as they are tactical. "Being wet 24/7, fighting through brush, crossing water — these little things have a huge impact on how you fight," Fonzi said. Over the course of the exercise, those small hardships become part of a larger test: whether multinational formations can adapt together in an environment that does not care how experienced, capable or well-equipped they were before entering it. That may ultimately be the most valuable lesson hidden beneath the canopy. Partnerships become meaningful when soldiers learn to depend on one another before circumstances require them to.

title: USS St. Louis Assumes U.S. Northern Command Mission at Southern Border
text: Maritime Security The littoral combat ship USS St. Louis departs Naval Station Mayport, Fla., in support of U.S. Northern Command's mission to secure the southern border of the United States, Sept. 13, 2026. Littoral combat ships are fast, agile, mission-focused platforms designed to operate in near-shore environments and defeat 21st century coastal threats, supporting the Navy's goals of forward presence, maritime security, sea control and deterrence. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.98 MB ) Credit: Navy Petty Officer 1st Class Keenan Daniels VIRIN: 260913-N-VW723-1260 The littoral combat ship USS St. Louis departed Naval Station Mayport, Florida, in support of U.S. Northern Command's mission to secure the southern border of the United States, Sept. 13. The St. Louis assumes duties previously executed by the USS Cooperstown in support of Northcom's border security objectives. The command is working together with the Department of Homeland Security to augment U.S. Customs and Border Protection along the southern border to disrupt illicit drug trafficking and protect the homeland. "Our crew has trained relentlessly for this deployment, and they stand ready for whatever challenges lie ahead. I could not be more proud to lead these sailors," said Navy Cmdr. Lester Shewmake, commanding officer of the USS St. Louis. "To our families and the Mayport community — thank you for your unwavering support as we head to sea." Navy assets are deployed under Northcom's maritime homeland defense authorities to enable maritime interdiction missions to prevent the flow of illegal drugs or other illegal activity. {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} The St. Louis is assigned to the Littoral Combat Ship Squadron 2 and homeported in Mayport. title: Hegseth, German Counterpart Agree to Advance Defense Industrial Cooperation
text: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Boris Pistorius, Germany's defense minister, met today at the Pentagon to discuss NATO 3.0, increased European defense spending and the defense industrial bases of both nations. "We're here to take another strong step in advancing our defense industrial cooperation between the United States and Germany," Hegseth said. Nato Partners The German, American and POW/MIA flags fly above Katterbach Army Airfield as U.S. Army AH-64E Apache helicopters fly in formation in Bavaria, Germany, Feb. 2, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.81 MB ) Credit: Army Spc. Grant Hockley VIRIN: 171230-A-GH759-4703 Last year at NATO headquarters in Brussels, Hegseth said allied nations must spend more on defense; President Donald J. Trump set the bar at 5% of gross domestic product. He added that increases in troop readiness, weapons production and force contributions were also needed. Hegseth, who calls the proposed changes NATO 3.0, said Germany has been "front and center" in making them happen. "Today, we see major progress that no one would have thought possible," he said. "Germany today is moving closer to fulfilling the 5% — leading the way on the spending commitment it made at the Hague Summit last year — but as we talked about, defense spending is just the first step." The secretary noted that increasing defense production on both sides of the Atlantic is essential. "NATO 3.0 will also require putting Germany's very large and historic industrial base to work for the common defense," Hegseth said. "It's the same thing that we're doing right here, as I and members of our team travel across the country; as we rebuild our arsenal of freedom." The arsenal of freedom plan, Hegseth said, aims to reindustrialize the U.S., rebuild American manufacturing, manufacture American-made products and create American jobs. The two civilian military leaders signed an agreement that, Hegseth said, aligns the War Department's acquisition transformation strategy with Germany's Procurement Acceleration Act. "When we align the two, you expand opportunities for joint development, production, licensed manufacturing, and expanded maintenance and sustainment capacities — exactly what allied countries should be doing," he said. "The objective is straightforward: Deliver capable systems to American, German and allied forces, at scale and at speed for maximum lethality." Pistorius highlighted Germany's immense increase in defense spending and said it's on board with the NATO 3.0 vision and with balancing out the burden of defending the NATO alliance. "Germany is strengthening its defense capabilities and acts as a driving force in Europe," he said. "We Europeans want to take some of the burden off the U.S. and assume primary responsibility for conventional deterrence in Europe." The German defense minister noted that since last year, Germany has increased defense spending by 25%, equivalent to about $147 billion. "We are investing in new state-of-the-art weapon systems here in the U.S.; we are assuming a leading role within NATO and, when it comes to providing support to Ukraine, we are strengthening NATO's eastern flank, particularly through our armored brigade in Lithuania," he said. He also highlighted German investments in technology, including space and deep-precision strike capabilities. Later this week, Germany will also roll out its first F-35A aircraft. The U.S.-Germany agreement, he said, will help Germany become an even stronger NATO partner than it has been for more than 70 years. "It creates a strong basis for closer armament cooperation between our two nations with one clear aim: increasing our production capacity," Pistorius said. He added that the NATO alliance must feature stronger European leadership to survive, and Germany will play a big part in that. "NATO needs to become more European in order to stay transatlantic," he said. "Burden shifting is progressing. Together with our allies, we are working towards a stronger Europe and a stronger NATO. And together with our American friends, we are working on strengthening our common defense and resilience." Spotlight: Acquisition Transformation Spotlight: NATO

title: Department of War Announces a $450 Million Investment in The Elmet Group to Secure America's Tungsten Supply Chain
text: The Department of War's Office of the Assistant Secretary of War for Industrial Base Policy, in partnership with the Economic Defense Unit, announced today a $450 million redeemable preferred equity investment in The Elmet Group through the Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment program. This strategic investment will strengthen domestic tungsten capacity, bolster U.S. industrial resilience and military readiness, and help secure an essential material for the defense industrial base. "This investment reflects the Department's commitment to rebuilding critical industrial capacity in the United States," said assistant secretary of War for industrial base policy Hon. Mike Cadenazzi. "Expanding domestic tungsten processing will strengthen supply chain resilience, support high-quality manufacturing jobs, and reinforce the production base behind essential defense systems." The Elmet Group is the only U.S.-owned, fully integrated producer of tungsten and molybdenum materials and components, supports more than 100 Department of War programs, including the F-35, Patriot PAC-3, Trident D5, NGI, PrSM, and Virginia- and Columbia-class submarines. Tungsten is a foundational input for the defense industrial base, prized for its hardness, heat resistance, density, and durability, and used in critical components across missiles, munitions, aerospace, propulsion, naval, undersea, electronics, and industrial manufacturing applications. "The Economic Defense Unit was created to identify critical industrial chokepoints before adversaries can exploit them and before they become battlefield risk," said George K. Kollitides II, director of the Economic Defense Unit. "Tungsten is essential to the systems that protect American warfighters and sustain deterrence, and this investment helps secure a domestic processing capability the United States cannot afford to leave exposed. By pairing targeted Department support with a disciplined preferred equity structure, we are strengthening the supply chain behind more than 100 defense programs while protecting taxpayers and delivering for the joint force." The Department's investment into Elmet will also establish the only independent ammonium paratungstate facility in North America, which is a key step for tungsten processing and one of the largest chokepoints across the U.S. industrial base. By expanding U.S.-aligned refining and processing capacity, this investment will help reduce reliance on adversary-dominated supply chains in markets where China currently dominates global supply, including an estimated 85 percent of tungsten and 40 percent of molybdenum. The Department's investment is expected to generate substantial economic benefits, including new high-tech jobs across Coldwater, Michigan, and Lewiston, Maine, preserving high-paying manufacturing jobs in Euclid, Ohio, and increasing demand for upstream mining jobs in Nevada. It is also expected to support approximately 1,200 downstream jobs across manufacturing, engineering, and logistics networks tied to major defense suppliers. The investment reflects the Department's broader strategy to secure critical industrial inputs, protect the defense supply chain, and ensure the United States can produce the materials required for sustained military advantage.

title: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth Speech on the Arsenal of Freedom in Oshkosh, WI
text: SECRETARY OF WAR PETE HEGSETH: How are we doing, Oshkosh? [Cheering] John, thank you very much for that gracious introduction and for everything that you do. And thank you all for being here. We're trying to be ahead of schedule for you here, not keep you waiting too long. I just had to go one extra lap on your training course on one of these beauties. They let me drive; it was nice. So, forgive me for being a little late. But I also want to thank our good friend here, a true ally of our warriors in Congress, Congressman Glenn Grothman. Glenn, where are you at? Glenn, thank you. Thank you. [Applause] President Trump talks a lot about 3 a.m. members of Congress, they call at 3 a.m. with extra demands before a key vote. Glenn is not a 3 a.m. guy; he's a reliable vote no matter what. Meaning when you need his vote, he's there to do the right thing on behalf of America First. Congressman, thank you very much. [Applause] Wisconsin's got a great delegation. I also want to thank a true warrior and a true patriot of the highest order, a friend of mine, Congressman Derrick Van Orden. He couldn't be here today, but he's a great advocate for what we stand for, as well as our good friend, Senator Ron Johnson, who runs the Senate Budget Committee; and I know is dedicated to ensuring in the coming weeks and months that the $350 billion reconciliation bill that's going to help fund our $1.5 trillion budget passes. So, Ron Johnson is a great ally, and we appreciate his support. I also want to thank a proud Wisconsinite, Undersecretary of War for Acquisitions and Sustainment, Mike Duffy. Mike, raise your hand. [Applause] Acquisitions and sustainment is like a mouthful of a title, but think of it this way, he is the War Department's official weapons buyer. He's the world's largest arms dealer and his name is Mike Duffy, Department of War. It is a great — great to be here with my team at Oshkosh in the great state of Wisconsin, home to 30,000 defense industrial base workers and 14,000 US service members. And I'm here on behalf of the commander-in-chief, Donald Trump, to say thank you for building faster and faster each day, the Arsenal of Freedom that our warriors need. I'm also here because I want an opportunity to look all of you in the eye, my fellow patriots, and tell you how important your job is. We don't have the helmets without the hard hats, and we don't have the warriors without the workers. We are all shoulder to shoulder in this Arsenal of Freedom. The vehicles you make here, as you know, are used by our warriors all around the world. Every single one of you, every welder, every receptionist to the CEO is supporting American warriors every single day. This is not just another manufacturing job; this is patriotism in the form of steel, past and present. It's incredible what you've accomplished here in Oshkosh. This company has played a role in every major conflict of the last 80 years since World War II. And I've seen your incredible work firsthand downrange, and I know that it saves American lives, the lives of American warriors. Many moons ago, I was a platoon leader in Iraq, fighting an enemy, a cowardly enemy that fought amongst women and children and hid IEDs with stand-off because they knew they couldn't fight American warriors toe to toe. And then Secretary of Defense Robert Gates, after my time in Iraq, but I went back a couple of times as an embedded reporter to see what the troops were up against during the Iraq surge. Robert Gates saw that they needed stronger, safer vehicles to protect our warriors. He cut the usual Pentagon red tape to get Oshkosh MRAPs to our warriors in theater. You and this company saved American lives. There are many American warriors — in fact, I have no doubt many veterans right here today living because of the good work of Midwest manufacturers like you. Their kids, someday their grandkids and their families, thank God, literally, for your work. It's a great American story that we are iterating on and replicating across our Department right now, and I'll explain more about that in a moment. But first, I think what's really special about Oshkosh is that 90 percent of your work is for commercial civilian use. It's great to see integrated production lines of both commercial and defense capabilities. At President Trump's Pentagon, unlike previous Pentagons, unlike what Joe Biden did at Obama did, commercial products and offerings are the default policy. We need more commercial companies in the Department of War space. We are open for business for the best American manufacturers, for all manufacturers. And you no longer have to sue your way into the Department in order to compete. Our job is to make it easier for the big guys and the little guys to get in to compete and ensure that American warriors have the best. You see, we came to Oshkosh because Oshkosh is a model for other commercial manufacturers to step up when your country needs you. From building the beautiful fire trucks I had a chance to see to the family of medium tactical vehicles; you are a model of delivering commercial and military capabilities to the warfighter. Most companies have been in the past too afraid, and rightfully so, of the maze of Pentagon bureaucracy. But I'm here to say we're a different kind of Department, moving at the speed of business, moving at the speed of markets, and we are open for business. We need more Oshkosh across America. During President Trump's first term in office, he rebuilt our military. Now, in his second term, he is rebuilding it yet again. A key piece of legislation passed by this Administration and championed by your representatives, the One Big, Beautiful Bill, specifically secured $190 million in defense contracts executed right here in Wisconsin. And we intend to do more as we move forward, modernizing our forces. This year's defense budget request includes $16.8 billion to modernize Army and Marine Corps combat equipment, which will include the procurement of new futuristic vehicles like the incredible Oshkosh Rogue Fires System. Just two months ago, the United States Marine Corps awarded Oshkosh a well-deserved $92 million contract for the rogue fires system. President Trump has promised a Golden Age of America, and he is delivering all across the country with American manufacturing and rebuilding our Defense Industrial Base. It's a part of the Trump economy that is booming, and that equates to jobs right here in your state and all across America. But I should note, selfishly, since at the War Department, we look at the metrics of our own people as well, that that also includes our military. Under the last Administration, military recruiting was at record lows. You see, they would miss a recruiting number so they would lower the goals and then they would miss that goal. And they would lower it so low that they could barely make it and then say they met their goal. But since November 2024, and something particular happened in November 2024, the U.S. military has seen its highest recruiting records in 30 years. Army, Air Force, Marine Corps, Navy, Space Force, you name it — and they're not just meeting goals, but we're exceeding them months and months in advance. And now with this $1.5 trillion bill, we're going to grow the size of each of those Services, and we're confident we'll meet those new goals as well. So, for the men and women looking to put on camouflage, the Department of War is open for business as well. And what a reflection of confidence from the American people, fathers and mothers to send their sons and daughters in record numbers to go serve. We're humbled by it and honored by it, and we'll continue to do right by them. And part of doing right by them is being right here with you. It's why building our Defense Industrial Base is part of our national defense strategy. It's why burden sharing is so fundamental to who we are and what we do. Every part of what we've focused on has been unleashing American business because we need the best weapons in the hands of warfighters. Right now, there are at least hundreds of thousands of jobs open in America's Defense Industrial Base, including jobs right here in Oshkosh. It was mentioned to me that there's a disproportionate number of vets that work here at this location and across Oshkosh. If you would, please raise your hand if you've served our country in uniform as well. God bless you. [Applause] Thank you. You guys and gals are serving again; it's an extension of service, just like everyone else next to you. You see, this administration knows that Midwest manufacturing doesn't just build our trucks or tanks or airplanes. American manufacturing built the middle class of the Midwest. American made, American manufacturing, American muscle, American money — funding it and in your pockets American jobs. Companies like Oshkosh combine American ingenuity with American work ethic, sheer American work ethic in support of our American warriors. It's an unbeatable combination that none of our adversaries can conceivably match. Well, that speed — I mentioned, Secretary Bob Gates, that was used for the MRAP program, is now what we are demanding for absolutely everything across the War Department. It is the norm, not the exception. We are cutting the red tape to get weapons to warriors in record time. You see, we're not just fighting adversaries. One of my jobs every single day is to go to war with the Pentagon bureaucracy. It is a war of attrition that we intend — our office intends to win. All four years we're going to cut red tape and requirements and ridiculous layers that have been added time and time again, year after year, mostly by lawyers of big companies that want to prevent competition. And we have to tear those barriers down to allow the best companies, America defense or commercial, large or small, to run as fast as possible. That's why we want all of our defense contractors to pivot and that's why we're doing this Arsenal of Freedom, to pivot to a wartime footing and build for victory. As I mentioned, for decades, the Pentagon was hampered by bureaucracy, bogged down by burdensome and inefficient processes, paralyzed by impossible risk thresholds, and distracted by agendas that had nothing to do with war fighting. It was mostly our fault; the world's largest bureaucracy, the Pentagon, sent contractors unstable demand signals. That's part of what we talked about on the factory floor today. Uncertain projections that made the defense industrial base risk averse, slow, lethargic, just like government. The companies that served government started looking like government, falling behind on budget, everything costing more. Ever changing an insane requirement, scheduling overruns became the norm, fat, lazy and complacent companies. Well, those days are over. Speed to delivery is now our organizing principle. We have slashed the culture of bureaucracy, ended the culture of risk aversion, and accelerating a culture of agility, innovation and sheer results. Process is not a result; all that matters is end state and results. No excuses; speed, scale, volume, efficiency, maximum urgency. Every dollar squandered on redundancy or bureaucracy or waste, it's an insult to you, the taxpayer and it's a theft from warfighters. This is a new Department with a new focus on our core mission, where we're restoring the warrior ethos. And that means a focus — an unrelenting, uncompromising focus on lethality. It means no more DEI. It means no more trannies, just training. It means colorblind, gender neutral, merit-based, back to basics across the board no matter if you're carrying a rifle or you're working on the plant floor. President Trump, in fact, he said when he gave me this job — moments afterwards, he said, Pete, I want you to bring the warriors back. [Laughter] Bring them back, and that's what we've done. That's been our focus — uncompromising, without apology from day one. And that's what the Arsenal of Freedom's been all about, bring American manufacturing and jobs and agility back. And that focus on lethality is reestablishing deterrence. We want a military so strong and powerful that our enemies never think about testing us. But as you know, our adversaries are not sitting idly by, they're moving fast. They're developing and delivering new capabilities at a rate that should be sobering for every single American. Which is why President Trump is asking our friends in Congress to pass a $1.5 trillion budget for our warriors. It is a bold, generational investment, the largest military budget in history but it's absolutely necessary. When you look under the hood and you understand the nature of the threat, you understand the negligence of previous Administrations, the deferred maintenance, it is what we must provide for the necessity of today's warriors and in order to make an investment in the future of warfare. Think autonomy and drones, AI, compute space, subsea, hyper sonics, cyber, you name it, we are laying the foundation for continued American dominance here at home, in our hemisphere and around the globe for decades to come, we will build the Arsenal of Freedom. And in the coming months, we will ensure that all of that $1.5 trillion is funded so that our department, working with great companies like this one, can provide it, and working with members of Congress who are willing to give us all the authorities. We need to give companies like Oshkosh stable, clear and consistent demand signals so that you can plan ahead, make more investments, and create more American jobs. I'll say it once and I'll say it again — no more offshoring, outsourcing — American made, American manufacturing, American muscle, American jobs. So, keep doing your part right here on the factory floor. We'll do our part at the Pentagon to keep cutting red tape, allowing you to run as fast as possible and speeding up the procurement process. And, you know, we all know, all of our warriors do their part every single day and every single night all around the world to keep us safe and they remain in our prayers constantly. So, thank you for delivering when it counted and continuing to deliver when it counts. Each one of you ought be proud, and your families, of what you do. Companies like this one are the backbone of the Arsenal of Freedom. Together we're going to guarantee peace through strength for generations to come, which is the point. So, God bless all of your families; God bless our warriors and our great republic. Thank you very much. [Applause]

title: Trump, Hegseth Commemorate 25th Anniversary of 9/11 at the Pentagon
text: President Donald J. Trump, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and other distinguished attendees commemorated the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on U.S. soil during a formal ceremony today in the Pentagon's courtyard. The two leaders were joined by First Lady Melania Trump; Air Force Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; and Condoleezza Rice, who served as secretary of state during 9/11. 1:34:07 During his remarks before a large gathering of guests that included survivors, first responders and family members of the victims, Trump honored the 184 victims of the attack on the Pentagon, the 2,573 who died in the World Trade Center attack and the 33 passengers who fought against their attackers on United Airlines Flight 93 over Shanksville, Pennsylvania. "Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago: we will never, ever forget," Trump said. The president also took time to honor all those who responded to the attacks in various capacities — both at the time of the attacks and in the years after — as well as those serving overseas today. "For 25 years, our best and bravest have kept America safe, and today, we salute every member of the United States military who served in the war on terror. … We salute our first responders and law enforcement — and we love them — and we salute the service members working right now to ensure the world's No. 1 sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never have a nuclear weapon," Trump said. Hegseth also spoke highly of those who are currently serving and those who have served over the past 25 years. "The top 1% of Americans — those that wear the uniform — still keep the watch, [and] we all sleep in peace because we know they stand ready," he said. The secretary added that, strengthened by faith, the military will continue to defeat the enemies of the U.S. and protect the republic, "just as the heroes and warriors of 9/11 did. Because, in this nation, in God we trust — in this land, in this place, on [9/11] — and still today," he said. {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} During his remarks, Caine reflected on being present at the Pentagon the day of the attacks, and on the many selfless acts he observed amid the chaos. "So many of us that day, who were here, saw courageous Americans giving that gift. And to the survivors and the families here today, your presence honors those that we lost … and reminds us of your strength — that we continued forward in this building, in New York, and around the country during one of our darkest chapters," Caine said. "We can't restore what was taken from us that day, but we can make and continue to hold a solemn promise: never to forget," he added. Rice spoke about her time in Washington on 9/11 and the resilience she saw afterward. "It is fitting that here at the Pentagon, we reflect not just on what happened here, but what — in that moment of crisis — people did here. They summoned a will and a spirit: a sense of obligation that our military lives by every day," she said. Prior to the remarks, the names of each of the 184 victims who lost their lives at the Pentagon were read aloud. The ceremony was preceded by an early-morning unfurling of the same American flag that was draped over the building's west wall the day after the 2001 attack. 13:10 Spotlight: Remembering September 11, 2001: 25 Years Later Experience: National 9/11 Pentagon Memorial Video: Pentagon Marks 25th Anniversary of 9/11 Video: Trump, DOW Leaders Host 9/11 Observance Ceremony

title: Hegseth Attends First Space Academy Commission Meeting
text: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth traveled to NASA's headquarters in Washington today where he attended the first meeting of the presidential commission on the U.S. Space Academy. President Donald J. Trump called for the development of a space academy via an Aug. 28 executive order . The order states that the space domain is critical to national security and that the nation must prepare the next generation of space professionals — including those in the military — in order to defend national interests. The commission, which is chaired by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, brings together senior leaders from the War Department, the Office of Management and Budget, and the National Security Council. During his brief remarks at the meeting's outset, Hegseth praised Isaacman and Air Force Secretary Troy Meink — both of whom attended — as well as President Trump for their leadership in getting the counsel assembled and on the path toward developing a space academy. "We are full speed ahead on this partnership on the United States Space Academy and the need for it. The president's been a leader in this domain from the beginning: the Space Force in the first term, [the] Space Academy in the second term," Hegseth said. Trump established the Space Force, which falls under the Department of the Air Force, Dec. 20, 2019, when the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2020 was signed into law. Hegseth went on to say that space is a domain that the U.S. can't just be "good at." "We need to dominate [in space]; and it's not just what we do at the War Department — it's what we do across government, at NASA, in private industry, in collaboration at every echelon," he said. "And so, we see this academy as a key component of ensuring we don't just lead, but we dominate." During his opening statement, Isaacson said that the U.S. is currently in another space race, namely with China and Russia, and that "success and failure comes down to months, not years." "This is why I think President Trump created the Space Force in his first term … and why now he has charged us to create the United States Space Academy: to make sure we have this training ground for the next generation of technicians, engineers, operators, pilots and astronauts to serve the needs of NASA, as well as the Space Force and other government agencies," he said. "Having an academy where we can train the next generation of space professionals — whether it be civilian or military — is just critically important," Meink said during his remarks. "So, we are really looking forward to working with [NASA] to make sure that happens, as well as just the increasing partnership we have [with] NASA across the board. ... I'm really looking forward to [the collaboration]." Per the executive order, the committee has until late December of this year to submit a report to the president proposing key details for the establishment of the academy.
